  "title": "Tokenization-Structure-Aware Process Rewards for Character-Level and Code-Level Reasoning via RLVR",
  "core_problem": "Current RLVR methods treat all tokens uniformly or weight by entropy, but remain agnostic to the fundamental role of tokenization structure in reasoning. When models must reason about sub-token content—spelling, counting, character manipulation, code identifier parsing—they need to correctly decompose tokens into characters or constituent subwords within their reasoning traces. Yet no RLVR method rewards correct decomposition or penalizes errors systematically correlated with BPE merge boundaries. This tokenization-structure blindness persists even in entropy-aware methods like ERPO, EP-GRPO, and EAPO, which identify high-stakes reasoning positions but cannot distinguish tokenization-induced errors from genuine reasoning failures. Sato & Sasano (EACL 2026) demonstrated that BPE merge rules are a primary factor in how models acquire character-level information, confirming that tokenization structure directly shapes—and constrains—sub-token reasoning capability. Mechanistically, Yang et al. (arXiv 2603.10771) showed that LLMs handle non-canonical (character-level) inputs by reconstructing word-level identities via specific internal subspaces, mediated by in-group attention among characters within the same canonical BPE token span—but this recovery mechanism is fragile (Llama-3.2-3B shows 35.8% accuracy degradation under character-level tokenization) and not explicitly trained. Critically, these tokenization-induced weaknesses are not confined to niche character puzzles: identifier renaming causes significant performance drops in code generation (ReCode documented 56-82% worst-case drops on 2023 models; recent evaluation on modern LLMs including Qwen2.5-Coder and Gemini-3 confirms persistent sensitivity, with Gemini-3 showing a 31.9pp drop from variable renaming alone, per arXiv 2505.10443), tokenization-fragmented entities degrade NER F1 by 8-20% ('Tokenization Falling Short', EMNLP 2024), and character-level perturbations (typos) cause up to 13% accuracy drops on mathematical reasoning (MGSM). These downstream consequences establish that sub-token reasoning failures have broad practical impact beyond character-counting tasks.",
  "opportunity": "Three converging developments make tokenization-structure-aware RLVR both tractable and timely. First, TASE (AAAI 2026, arXiv:2508.05468) demonstrated that standard GRPO applied to token-awareness tasks improved Qwen2.5-14B's Token Awareness score from 13.65% to 25.11% (+11.46% absolute) using only outcome-level rewards—validating that RLVR can improve token-level understanding while suggesting substantial headroom for process-level reward shaping. Second, the diagnostic literature has matured: 'Say Anything but This' (arXiv 2601.14658) taxonomized 8 systematic tokenizer artifacts causing phantom edits across 10 LLMs, 'The Strawberry Problem' (arXiv 2505.14172) showed character decomposition emerges late and is vocabulary-dependent, TokDrift (arXiv 2510.14972) demonstrated that identifier renaming causes 9.26% average sensitivity across code LLMs with up to 60% change rates for individual naming convention rules, and Sato & Sasano (EACL 2026, arXiv 2602.05347) proved that BPE merge rules are the primary tokenization-dependent factor in character knowledge acquisition—collectively establishing that tokenization-induced errors are systematic, classifiable, and cross-domain. Third, the theoretical foundation for entropy-gated credit assignment is now established: He et al. (arXiv 2604.11056) proved via Conditional Mutual Information that the credit a token can carry is upper-bounded by its entropy, GRPO-VPS (ICLR 2026) showed that adding segment-level verifiable signals to GRPO improves accuracy by up to 2.6 points while reducing reasoning length by 35.9%, and Execution-Grounded Credit Assignment (arXiv 2603.16158, ICLR 2026 Workshop SPOT) demonstrated that localizing GRPO advantage to specific token spans via execution traces improves code generation by +3.1 on HumanEval—establishing that fine-grained, structurally-informed credit assignment outperforms uniform reward distribution. Fourth, a mechanistic basis for downstream transfer has emerged: Yang et al. (arXiv 2603.10771) identified word recovery subspaces that reconstruct canonical token identities from character-level inputs, mediated by in-group attention within BPE token boundaries—providing a concrete neural mechanism that TSA-GRPO's boundary-aware training could strengthen. Shi et al. (arXiv 2604.25011) showed that RL fine-tuning identifies and strengthens compact, task-relevant features that mediate cross-task generalization, and that amplifying these features improves base model performance—suggesting that TSA-GRPO's process rewards targeting decomposition at BPE boundaries could selectively strengthen word recovery representations, producing downstream robustness benefits. The gap remains: no method uses tokenization structure itself as the process verification signal.",
  "landscape": "GRPO (DeepSeek-R1) uses rule-based outcome verifiers. GTPO (arXiv 2508.04349) assigns entropy-weighted token-level rewards. λ-GRPO (arXiv 2510.06870) learns token preferences. ERPO (arXiv 2603.28204) introduces entropy-aware gating at Critical Decision Pivots via an adaptive sigmoid gating function, achieving +4.69% on AMC23 over GRPO—but remains tokenization-structure-agnostic. EP-GRPO (arXiv 2605.04960, May 2026) combines entropy-gated modulation with implicit process signals derived from policy divergence, achieving +26.4% relative improvement (+4.79pp absolute, from 18.14% to 22.93% average accuracy) over GRPO on Qwen2.5-3B math tasks—sharing our entropy-gating intuition but deriving process signals self-supervisedly from policy divergence rather than from tokenization structure, and targeting math reasoning rather than character/code domains. He et al. (arXiv 2604.11056) proved that token-level credit is upper-bounded by entropy via Conditional Mutual Information and proposed EAPO (Entropy-Aware Policy Optimization)—providing theoretical justification for concentrating process rewards at high-entropy positions, which we adopt for our CDR/TBP gating. GRPO-VPS (ICLR 2026) adds verifiable process supervision via confidence probing at segment boundaries, but its verification is domain-general. Execution-Grounded Credit Assignment (arXiv 2603.16158, ICLR 2026 Workshop SPOT) localizes GRPO advantage to specific token spans via execution trace comparison, achieving +3.1 on HumanEval with 18% overhead—demonstrating that structurally-informed credit assignment in code generation outperforms uniform distribution, though using execution divergence rather than tokenization structure as the localization signal. High-entropy token gating (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2506.01939) shows training on only 20% high-entropy tokens retains full performance. On the tokenization-awareness side: TIPA (ACL 2025, arXiv 2411.17679) uses auxiliary reverse character prediction to improve character-position awareness—producing both implicit character awareness and demonstrated transfer to Chinese Spelling Correction (10% improvement over baselines), establishing that character-level training can benefit downstream tasks. StochasTok (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2506.01687) modifies tokenization itself by randomly splitting tokens with probability p=0.1, achieving dramatic character-task improvements at 50M-275M scale—but requires tokenization pipeline modification, has not been demonstrated at >1B scale, and the authors explicitly note that downstream evaluation on 'coding, algebra, or scientific reasoning' remains future work. Sato & Sasano (EACL 2026, arXiv 2602.05347) analyzed how LMs acquire character-level information through controlled experiments varying pre-training datasets and tokenizers, finding that BPE merge rules and orthographic constraints are the primary tokenization-dependent factors—directly supporting our design of TBP around merge boundaries. 'Say Anything but This' (arXiv 2601.14658) provides a taxonomy of 8 tokenizer artifacts across 10 LLMs and shows scaling alone cannot resolve tokenization-rooted deficiencies. TASE (AAAI 2026, arXiv:2508.05468) trained Qwen2.5-14B with GRPO on token-awareness tasks, improving Token Awareness from 13.65% to 25.11%—validating RLVR for token-level understanding but using only outcome rewards. TokDrift (arXiv 2510.14972) introduced semantic-preserving rewrite rules (6 naming convention transformations: camelCase↔snake_case↔PascalCase↔SCREAMING_CASE) showing 9.26% average sensitivity and up to 60% output change rates from identifier renaming alone in code LLMs—directly motivating our code identifier evaluation domain. On mechanistic understanding: Yang et al. (arXiv 2603.10771) identified word recovery subspaces that reconstruct canonical BPE token identities from character-level inputs, showing that in-group attention among characters within the same canonical token is critical for this reconstruction (masking it in early layers substantially degrades task performance), with recovery scores ranging from 57.7% to 96.8% across models—Qwen2.5-7B shows a two-stage recovery pattern with sharp increases in mid-to-late layers, directly suggesting that training interventions targeting these layers could strengthen recovery. Shi et al. (arXiv 2604.25011) provided causal evidence that RL fine-tuning identifies compact, task-agnostic features mediating generalization: disabling these features degrades RL models' performance, while amplifying them improves base models—establishing that RL can selectively strengthen task-relevant internal representations. On downstream robustness: ReCode (ACL 2023) demonstrated that semantic-preserving code perturbations including variable/identifier renaming cause substantial performance drops (56-82% worst-case on 2023 models CodeGen/InCoder; recent evaluation by arXiv 2505.10443 on modern LLMs including Qwen2.5-Coder, Qwen3-Coder, and Gemini-3 confirms persistent sensitivity, with Gemini-3 showing a 31.9pp drop from variable renaming and loop unrolling causing 35-44pp drops); 'Tokenization Falling Short' (EMNLP 2024) showed that subword splits reduce robustness on perturbed inputs, with F1 drops of 8-20%; and CREME (ICSE 2026) showed that targeted layer-level editing at robustness-sensitive layers (concentrated in middle and deeper layers, overlapping with where Qwen2.5's word recovery sharply increases) can recover 63% of perturbed-prompt accuracy on code generation—demonstrating that tokenization-sensitive robustness is both measurable and improvable at the representation level. CBRL (arXiv 2603.18953) addresses the cold-start problem via few-shot demonstration injection with annealing curriculum. The Divide-and-Conquer approach (arXiv 2502.08180) improves character manipulation via prompting without training. No paper found as of May 2026 combines tokenization-structure-aware process rewards with RLVR for character-level or code-level reasoning, nor evaluates whether such improvements transfer to downstream robustness tasks.",
  "inspired_by": "Combination: merging RLVR process-level reward shaping (GRPO-VPS's verifiable process supervision, ERPO/EP-GRPO's entropy-aware gating, the theoretical credit-entropy bound from arXiv 2604.11056, EGCA's execution-grounded token-span credit assignment) with tokenization-structure diagnostics (TIPA's character-position awareness and CSC transfer, 'Say Anything but This' artifact taxonomy, TokDrift's identifier boundary misalignment, Sato & Sasano's BPE merge rule analysis) and a mechanistic transfer pathway (Yang et al.'s word recovery subspaces mediated by in-group attention within BPE boundaries, Shi et al.'s evidence that RL selectively strengthens task-relevant features) and downstream robustness evidence (ReCode's identifier-renaming performance drops confirmed on modern LLMs, 'Tokenization Falling Short' perturbation sensitivity, CREME's layer-level robustness recovery) to create tokenization-structure-aware process rewards for RLVR with mechanistically motivated downstream transfer. Gap: the entire RLVR literature—including recent entropy-aware methods (ERPO, GTPO, EP-GRPO, EAPO) and execution-grounded methods (EGCA)—ignores tokenization structure; the tokenization-awareness literature (StochasTok, TIPA) uses supervised or tokenizer-modification approaches and defers downstream evaluation; the word recovery literature identifies the mechanism but proposes no training-time strengthening; the code robustness literature (ReCode, CREME) diagnoses and patches the problem at inference time but proposes no training-time solution; and the code tokenization literature (TokDrift) diagnoses the problem but proposes no training-time solution.",
  "approach": "We propose TSA-GRPO (Tokenization-Structure-Aware GRPO), which augments GRPO with two novel tokenization-aware process reward signals, trained via a three-phase curriculum with explicit phase transition criteria that address the bootstrapping challenge. We evaluate on both character-level tasks (primary) and code identifier manipulation tasks (secondary), and additionally perform downstream transfer evaluations to test the mechanistically motivated hypothesis that boundary-aware training strengthens word recovery representations.

**Phase 1: Character Decomposition Seeding (CD-Seed, ~3 weeks).** We fine-tune Qwen3-8B-Base on a curated dataset of character-level and code identifier task solutions containing explicit decomposition traces (e.g., character: 'How many r's in strawberry? Let me spell it out: s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y. Counting r's: positions 4, 9, 10. Answer: 3'; code: 'Split getUserName into words: get-User-Name. That's 3 words.'). This addresses the critical bootstrapping problem: TIPA produces implicit awareness via reverse JSON prediction but does not induce explicit decomposition in reasoning traces, and 'The Strawberry Problem' shows such decomposition does not emerge naturally. We augment CD-Seed with TIPA-style auxiliary tasks and adopt CBRL-inspired few-shot demonstration injection (starting at 50% injection probability, annealing to 0% over training) to bootstrap decomposition behavior before transitioning to RL.

**Phase Transition Criterion (Phase 1 → Phase 2):** Advance when two conditions are jointly met on a held-out validation set of 500 character/code tasks: (a) ≥60% of sampled model outputs contain a recognizable decomposition pattern (measured by CDR Tier 1 + Tier 2 combined match rate), indicating the model has learned to produce explicit decomposition traces; AND (b) outcome accuracy on held-out character tasks exceeds 20%, ensuring the model can produce correct answers and not merely decomposition-formatted noise. These thresholds are motivated by the observation that TASE's baseline Qwen2.5-14B achieved only 13.65% Token Awareness without any character-focused training, so 20% represents a meaningful improvement from CD-Seed; the 60% decomposition rate ensures sufficient signal density for CDR/TBP to provide informative gradients during Phase 2.

**Phase 2: Structure-Aware RLVR (~6 weeks).** We apply TSA-GRPO with two process reward components, each using a two-tier verification architecture designed to handle format drift during RL exploration:

(1) Character Decomposition Reward (CDR): A two-tier verifier that detects and evaluates character decomposition steps in reasoning traces.
  - Tier 1 (Pattern-Matched): Parameterized regex patterns recognize known decomposition formats: hyphenated ('s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y'), numbered ('1:s, 2:t, ...'), spaced ('s t r a w b e r r y'), enumerated lists, and code identifier splits ('get-User-Name'). When matched, the extracted sequence is verified against ground truth, and CDR assigns reward proportional to character-level accuracy (Levenshtein similarity).
  - Tier 2 (Fallback Edit-Distance): When no Tier 1 pattern matches—critical for handling format drift as RL exploration generates novel decomposition styles—CDR applies a sliding-window character extraction heuristic that identifies candidate decomposition substrings in the trace (sequences with high character overlap with the target), computes Levenshtein similarity against ground truth, and assigns a discounted reward (scaled by 0.5× relative to Tier 1) to maintain non-zero signal. This is inspired by TinyV's (arXiv 2505.14625) demonstration that reducing false negatives in RLVR verification improves training by up to 10% via preserving informative gradient signals.
  - Adaptive Pattern Registry: Every 500 training steps, we sample 200 model outputs, cluster novel decomposition formats not matched by Tier 1, and promote frequently-occurring formats (>5% prevalence) to Tier 1 with auto-generated regex patterns. This ensures the pattern library co-evolves with model behavior.

(2) Tokenization Boundary Penalty (TBP): An algorithmic pipeline that detects reasoning errors correlated with BPE merge boundaries:
  (a) BPE-segment the target string using the model's tokenizer to obtain token list and character-level boundary positions (e.g., 'strawberry' → ['str', 'aw', 'berry'] → boundaries at positions {3, 5}). For code identifiers, additionally identify word boundaries from naming conventions (e.g., 'getUserName' → word boundaries at {3, 7}).
  (b) Parse the model's character-by-character enumeration from the reasoning trace using CDR-detected decomposition.
  (c) Compute Levenshtein alignment between the model's enumerated characters and ground truth, identifying insertion/deletion/substitution errors with their positions.
  (d) Classify each error as boundary-proximal (within ±1 character position of a BPE merge boundary or word boundary) or boundary-distal. The ±1 threshold is motivated by the 'off-by-one' error pattern documented in 'Say Anything but This' and is treated as a hyperparameter with ±0 and ±2 included in sensitivity analysis.
  (e) Apply weighted penalty: P_TBP = β · (2 · n_proximal + n_distal), where β is the overall TBP weight and the 2:1 proximal-to-distal ratio is fixed (not tuned), providing stronger gradient signal for tokenization-correlated errors.

**Mechanistic Motivation for Downstream Transfer.** TSA-GRPO's process rewards are designed to strengthen the word recovery mechanism identified by Yang et al. (arXiv 2603.10771). Their work showed that LLMs reconstruct canonical BPE token identities from character-level inputs via in-group attention among characters within the same token span, and that this mechanism is causally necessary for downstream task performance. CDR directly rewards correct character-to-token decomposition at BPE boundaries, while TBP penalizes errors at boundary-proximal positions—both providing gradient signal precisely at the positions where in-group attention must correctly aggregate character information. Shi et al. (arXiv 2604.25011) showed that RL fine-tuning identifies and strengthens compact, task-relevant features that mediate cross-task generalization, with causal evidence that amplifying these features improves base model performance. We hypothesize that TSA-GRPO's boundary-aware process rewards selectively strengthen word recovery subspaces, producing more robust sub-token representations that transfer to downstream tasks where tokenization fragmentation degrades performance. CREME's finding that robustness-sensitive layers in code LLMs are concentrated in middle and deeper layers—overlapping with where Qwen2.5's word recovery shows sharp increases—further suggests that the representations TSA-GRPO targets are precisely those that mediate code generation robustness.

**Simplified Hyperparameter Design.** To address the risk of a high-dimensional tuning space, we adopt a hierarchical parameterization that reduces effective search dimensionality. The per-token advantage combines standard GRPO group advantage with modulated process signals: A_{i,t} = A_i^{GRPO} + w(H_t) · λ_process · (CDR_{i,t} + TBP_{i,t}), where: (i) w(H_t) is the entropy-dependent gating function from ERPO with fixed default parameters (γ_gate=5, δ=1e-6), theoretically justified by the credit-entropy upper bound (arXiv 2604.11056); (ii) λ_process is the single tunable process reward scale controlling the overall influence of CDR+TBP relative to outcome advantage; (iii) the β_prox:β_dist ratio within TBP is fixed at 2:1; (iv) the ±1 boundary-proximal threshold is fixed. This reduces the effective hyperparameter search to λ_process (1D grid search over {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0}) plus standard GRPO hyperparameters, dramatically simplifying tuning compared to the naïve 5+ dimensional space.

**Phase Transition Criterion (Phase 2 → Phase 3):** Advance when two conditions are jointly met: (a) CDR Tier 1 match rate exceeds 80% on training outputs, indicating the model has converged to stable, recognizable decomposition patterns rather than relying on Tier 2 fallback; AND (b) the process reward contribution to advantage has stabilized, measured as the coefficient of variation of λ_process · mean(CDR + TBP) falling below 0.15 over the last 1000 training steps. The 80% Tier 1 threshold ensures decomposition behavior is well-internalized before removing process supervision; the stability criterion prevents premature transition during periods of active learning.

**Phase 3: Consolidation (~2 weeks).** Standard GRPO with outcome rewards; λ_process decays linearly to zero over training, allowing the model to internalize decomposition behavior without ongoing process supervision.

We train on a multi-task RLVR curriculum spanning CharBench (counting + indexing), TASE (10 tasks), SubTokenTest (4 domains), and CodeIdBench (our new code identifier benchmark), using OpenRLHF.",
  "downstream_transfer_evaluation": "**Downstream Transfer Evaluations: Mechanistically Motivated Hypothesis Tests.** A key question is: 'Why should we care about better character counting?' We answer this with a mechanistic argument and two hypothesis-testing evaluations. The mechanistic bridge: Yang et al. (arXiv 2603.10771) showed LLMs reconstruct word-level identities from character inputs via word recovery subspaces, mediated by in-group attention among characters within canonical BPE token spans. TSA-GRPO's CDR/TBP training provides gradient signal precisely at BPE boundary positions where this in-group attention must correctly aggregate—we hypothesize this selectively strengthens word recovery representations. Shi et al. (arXiv 2604.25011) provided causal evidence that RL fine-tuning identifies and strengthens compact, task-relevant features mediating generalization, supporting our prediction that boundary-aware process rewards will produce downstream-transferable representation improvements.

**(1) Code Generation Robustness via ReCode-Rename (Hypothesis Test).** We evaluate TSA-GRPO-trained models on ReCode's (ACL 2023) identifier-renaming perturbation suite applied to HumanEval and MBPP. Note on temporal context: ReCode's original 56-82% worst-case drops were measured on 2023 models (CodeGen, InCoder); recent evaluation on modern LLMs (arXiv 2505.10443, testing Qwen2.5-Coder, Qwen3-Coder, GPT-5.2, Gemini-3) confirms persistent sensitivity to semantics-preserving mutations, with Gemini-3 showing a 31.9pp drop from variable renaming alone and loop unrolling causing 35-44pp drops in Qwen models. Our downstream evaluation will measure actual robustness drops on current-generation models as the baseline. Hypothesis: models trained with TSA-GRPO that have learned to correctly decompose identifiers at BPE boundaries—and been penalized for boundary-proximal errors via TBP-Code—should exhibit strengthened word recovery subspaces (per the Yang et al. mechanism), leading to more robust internal representations of identifier structure and greater resilience when identifiers are renamed. This evaluation requires zero additional training; we simply evaluate our TSA-GRPO checkpoint on the perturbed benchmark. We report: (a) Pass@1 on clean HumanEval vs. GRPO baseline (to verify no degradation), (b) Robust Drop (RD) on ReCode-Rename perturbations vs. GRPO baseline (primary metric), (c) per-perturbation-type breakdown to identify which renaming strategies TSA-GRPO handles better, and (d) word recovery probe: we apply the Yang et al. decoding-based recovery analysis to compare word recovery scores between TSA-GRPO and GRPO checkpoints at each layer, testing whether TSA-GRPO indeed produces higher recovery scores (direct mechanistic validation). Expected outcome: ≥15% relative reduction in Robust Drop compared to GRPO baseline. However, we frame this as a hypothesis test: even if the improvement is smaller or null, the result is informative—it delineates the transfer boundary of tokenization-structure-aware training and indicates whether word recovery strengthening alone is sufficient for code generation robustness, or whether additional interventions (e.g., CREME-style layer editing) are needed in conjunction.

**(2) Character Perturbation Resilience via TypoRobust (Hypothesis Test).** We evaluate on character-perturbed inputs following the protocol of 'Tokenization Falling Short' (EMNLP 2024) and 'On the Ability of LLMs to Handle Character-Level Perturbations' (arXiv 2510.14365). We apply controlled character-level perturbations (substitution, insertion, deletion at rates of 5% and 10% per character) to inputs from GSM8K and a subset of MMLU, measuring accuracy degradation relative to clean inputs. Hypothesis: models that have learned explicit character decomposition through TSA-GRPO should have stronger word recovery subspaces (Yang et al. showed these mediate robustness to non-canonical character-level inputs), making them more resilient to character-level noise. We report: (a) clean accuracy (to verify no degradation), (b) accuracy under 5% and 10% perturbation rates vs. GRPO baseline, (c) relative accuracy retention (perturbed/clean ratio), and (d) word recovery probe comparing recovery scores between TSA-GRPO and GRPO checkpoints under perturbed inputs. Expected outcome: ≥10% relative improvement in accuracy retention under 10% character perturbation compared to GRPO baseline. As with ReCode-Rename, null results are informative: they would suggest that explicit character decomposition training strengthens character-level reasoning but does not transfer to input-level noise robustness, pointing to a distinction between output-side decomposition capability and input-side perturbation resilience.

These downstream evaluations are lightweight (evaluation-only, no additional training, ~30 GPU-hours total for benchmarks + ~10 GPU-hours for word recovery probes) and transform the downstream transfer claim from 'plausible hypothesis' to 'mechanistically motivated prediction with direct neural-level validation.'",
  "code_identifier_evaluation": "**CodeIdBench: A Committed Secondary Evaluation Domain.** We construct CodeIdBench, a benchmark of ~500 code identifier manipulation tasks directly motivated by TokDrift's findings. Tasks are drawn from identifiers in HumanEval and CodeNet codebases and span four task types:

(1) Identifier Word Splitting: Given a compound identifier (e.g., 'getUserName', 'sorted_list_copy'), decompose into constituent words (['get', 'User', 'Name']). This directly probes whether the model can reason about sub-token structure within identifiers.

(2) Naming Convention Conversion: Convert identifiers between camelCase, snake_case, PascalCase, and SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (mirroring TokDrift's 6 rewrite rules N1-N6). Requires correct word boundary identification followed by format transformation.

(3) Character Counting within Identifiers: Count specific characters or total characters in identifiers where BPE segmentation fragments the identifier unpredictably.

(4) Word Extraction: Extract the nth word from a compound identifier (e.g., 'the 2nd word of getUserName is User').

All tasks use exact string matching for verifiable rewards. CDR and TBP are adapted for code: CDR-Code verifies identifier-to-word decomposition traces; TBP-Code detects errors at BPE boundaries within identifiers (e.g., 'getUserName' might be tokenized as ['get', 'User', 'Name'] or ['getUser', 'Name'], and TBP penalizes errors near the {3, 7} or {7} boundary sets respectively). We target >5% absolute improvement over GRPO baseline on CodeIdBench, establishing that tokenization-structure-aware process rewards generalize beyond character-level tasks to code domains.",
  "generalization_beyond_primary_domains": "Beyond our committed evaluation on character-level tasks, code identifier manipulation, and downstream transfer (code robustness and typo resilience), the TSA-GRPO framework introduces a general principle: incorporating tokenization structure into RLVR reward signals wherever tokenization boundaries systematically cause errors. We identify two additional generalization directions supported by existing evidence: (1) Multilingual processing: tokenization is particularly problematic for morphologically rich and low-resource languages, where BPE merges fragment meaningful morphemes; 'Tokenization Matters' (arXiv 2504.16977) showed that BPE's poor handling of morphological complexity limits zero-shot NER transfer for Indic languages, suggesting process rewards that detect morpheme-boundary errors could improve multilingual reasoning. (2) Structured output generation: JSON/XML generation where token boundaries may cut across field names, delimiters, or values. These remain exploratory directions for future work; our primary contribution demonstrates the principle via character and code domains, with mechanistically motivated downstream transfer evaluations bridging to practical applications.",
